## Preserving Information in Quantum Systems via Coherent Driving

Abstract

Among the fundamental phenomena that characterize a quantum system is coherent superposition between states, which we can write for a two-level system as:

|ψ⟩= α|0⟩+ eiφβ|1⟩. (1)

A superposition is characterized by a phase φ which can be difficult to conceptualize with our physical intuition, trained only by experience in a classical world. Perhaps we can best approach it by considering the phase of classical waves, which we can concretely visualize, andwhichleadtosomeanalogousphenomenalikeinterference. Ineffectthere is additional information in the system beyond the probability that it is measured in one state vs. the other. Thisphaseis botha resourceand avulnerability of quantum systems. On one hand, it gives the system another degree of freedom which we can control. On the other hand, it can be easily lost, since the phase of a superposition tends to be very sensitive to fluctuations in the system’s surrounding environment. The length of time that the phase remains known in a system (or equivalently, that the system maintains its information) is called the coherence time. In this thesis I will discuss two examples in which a coherent superposition of states is used to preserve information in a quantum system. In both cases the key laboratory tool used to access the quantum system is an AC field of classical amplitude which coherently drives the states, and in both cases we will see the beneficial properties of the stationary solutions of the combined system plus field, which are superposition states (in the basis that does not include the field). Chapter 1 will deal with an example of a coherent field extending the coherence time of a two-level system. I will show experimental data demonstrating this effect in the electron spin of the silicon vacancy in diamond, where the coherent driving field is a strain field in the carbon lattice. Chapter 2 will explain how the decay channels of a single atomic system can be controlled using superpositions of states, a phenomena which could be used to increase the fidelity of a state measurement. These results are computational rather than experimental, but I will suggest a real quantum system in which this phenomena could be demonstrated and calculate expected results.

### 1.1 Introduction

Thenegatively-chargedsiliconvacancy(SiV)centerindiamondcomprisesasiliconatom

located interstitially between two vacancies in the carbon lattice. By defining a qubit

on its ground state electron spin levels, which are coherent at cryogenic temperature, it

can be used to store quantum information. It has the additional benefits of stability in

nanostructures, and optical transitions which allow its state to be optically initialized

and read out. Of particular interest to this dissertation, however, is the uniquely high

strain response (1 PHz/strain) of the SiV’s optical and orbital energy levels2,3. Because

of spin-orbit coupling the qubit spin states have an orbital characteristic, so in the pres-

ence of an off-axis magnetic field, they also couple to strain. Static strain fields can be

used to tune the energy states of the SiV, which is especially useful for the optical tun-

ing because the SiV is first-order insensitive to electric Stark tuning which is commonly

used in related defects3. Alternatively, an oscillating strain field can be used to reso-

nantely and coherently drive the SiV’s spin with impressively large strain response of

∼100 THz/strain2,4. (We note that oscillation strain fields resonant with the spin tran-

sition can also have off-resonant effects on the orbital and optical states (see sections 1.7

and 1.5.1)). The potential for large couplings between SiV spins and coherent phonons

holds great promise for exploring the emerging field of quantum phononics.

The phonon is an intriguing up-and-coming candidate as a quantum information

carrier in on-chip quantum communications. It holds several distinct advantages over

its electromagnetic cousin the photon:

• Because the speed of sound is ∼4-5 orders of magnitude slower than the speed of

light, a phonon has a much shorter wavelength than a photon of the same fre-

quency, enabling smaller device footprints and many more devices on a chip.

### 2.1 Introduction

Optical cycling transitions are an important feature of atomic systems, allowing high-

fidelity state measurement in solid-state quantum defects34,35,36,11, as well as trapped

ions and atoms37,38,39. Cycling transitions are additionally used to cool and trap atoms

and ions40,41,42,43. Deviation from ideal cyclicity due to additional spurious decay chan-

nels decreases the fidelity of state readout44,34 and reduces the efficiency of cooling and

trapping. The pursuit of improved cyclicity in optical transitions has lead to recent

advances in molecular design45,46,47,48 and demonstrations of selective cavity enhance-

ment of optical transitions36,49. This relies, however, on the cavity linewidth being nar-

rower than the spectral separation between the desired decay paths and the undesired

decay paths, which may be technologically infeasible. This chapter will discuss another

means of increasing cyclicity, which leverages the coherent interference of decay paths,

controlled via externally applied driving fields.

The phenomenon of coherent interference of decay has been proposed for tailor-

ing of spectral lineshapes50,51, population inversion for lasing purposes52, and squeez-

ing51. It is closely related to coherent population trapping53, though coherent popula-

tion trapping is usually framed in terms of a dark superposition state which cannot be

populated by an applied field, whereas interference of decay involves a dark superposi-

tion state which does not spontaneously decay.

This chapter will focus on the relative enhancement and suppression of different

### 2.10 Discussion

We have proposed and analyzed two methods for enhancing the cyclicity of optical tran-

sitions in atomic systems by exploiting the coherent interference of decay paths. The

first, a strong-drive scheme, relies on a certain phase and amplitude relationship between

the bare state transition dipole moments. Under these conditions, a single strong driv-

ing field will effectively drive the system between a ground state and an excited state

superposition that decays only to that ground state. Using the negatively charged nickel

vacancy center in diamond as a concrete example, we demonstrated that this approach

can enable high-fidelity optical readout even under misaligned magnetic fields, where

inherent cycling transitions do not exist.

The second method, the auxiliary-drive scheme, requires an additional metastable

statecoupledtotheexcitedstatemanifold,whichallowsfine-tunedcontrolofthedressed-

state composition via the amplitude and detuning of an auxiliary field. This approach

relaxes the stringent requirements on transition dipole moments and drive strength im-

posed by the strong-drive scheme, while maintaining the ability to coherently suppress

undesired decay channels. Simulations show that appropriate tuning of the auxiliary

field can sustain continuous photon cycling and high emission counts at moderate op-

tical powers.

Together, these methods provide a general framework for engineering effective cy-

cling transitions in a wide range of atomic and solid-state systems, including color cen-

ters, trapped ions, and molecular emitters. By leveraging quantum interference in the

decay process, they circumvent the need for narrow optical cavities or highly selective

transitions, offering a scalable route to improved optical readout fidelity in quantum

technologies.
